vignette:
Alex sits at his desk, the blue light of a dual-monitor setup illuminating the sharp lines of his face. The numbers on the spreadsheet are supposed to be his world-a logical, predictable universe of risk assessment and market trends where he has always been king. But today, the columns of data swim before his eyes, meaningless. He's not in his corner office in Chicago; he's in the dark again, the rough fabric of a hood over his head, the smell of damp earth and unwashed bodies filling his nostrils. The memory, uninvited and visceral, lasts only a second, but it leaves him breathless, his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird.

Five years ago, Alex was on top of his game. He had just closed a major deal, and to celebrate, he and his then-wife, Sarah, took a trip to South America-a hiking excursion he'd meticulously planned. He remembers the feeling of the sun on his face on that last morning, the satisfaction of a challenge met. That feeling was the last pure, uncomplicated joy he can recall. The abduction happened on a remote trail. It was brutally efficient. They were not political targets, just Westerners in the wrong place at the wrong time, their value calculated in dollars.

For nineteen days, he was held in a small, windowless room with two other hostages. Time ceased to be linear, measured only by the infrequent delivery of food and water and the terrifying uncertainty of footsteps outside the door. He learned the true meaning of helplessness, a concept entirely foreign to a man who built his life on control and foresight. He'd spend hours analyzing the patterns of his captors' movements, their tones of voice, trying to build a predictive model for survival in his head. It was a futile exercise. His life was a variable in someone else's equation, and he had no control over the outcome.

The rescue was as chaotic and violent as the capture. The sudden noise, the shouting in a language he didn't understand, the blinding light-it was liberation, but it felt like just another assault. Back home, everyone expected him to be grateful, relieved. And he was, for a while. But the relief was a thin veneer over a chasm of terror. The world no longer felt solid beneath his feet.

Sarah tried. She encouraged him to talk, to take time off, to see someone. But he couldn't form the words. The experience was a locked box inside him, and speaking of it felt like giving it power, letting it out into the world he was desperately trying to re-inhabit. Instead, he threw himself back into his work, seeking refuge in the cold logic of finance. But the man who returned to the office was not the same. He became irritable, his patience worn to a brittle edge. He'd flinch violently if a colleague came up behind him too quietly. He insisted on a desk in the corner, where no one could pass behind him, and he'd find himself scanning the faces of strangers on the train, assessing threats that weren't there.

The nights were the worst. He would wake up drenched in sweat, the phantom feeling of confinement pressing in on him, his own bedroom feeling like a cell. He started sleeping on the couch, needing the open space of the living room. Sarah began to feel like she was living with a ghost. His emotional detachment, punctuated by sudden, inexplicable flashes of anger, eroded their marriage until it crumbled. He doesn't blame her for leaving; he had already left her long before she packed her bags.

Now, at 37, his world has shrunk to the predictable path between his sterile apartment and his fortified corner of the office. He no longer travels, avoids crowded places, and hasn't been on a hiking trail since. The numbers on the screen are his only remaining sanctuary, a place where outcomes can be calculated and risks can be managed. Yet, even here, the ghosts find him. He closes his eyes, takes a shaky breath, and forces his focus back to the spreadsheet, trying to impose an order on his screen that he can no longer find anywhere else.
